utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. For the record, all the accused are here. Representation, Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Mitchell for the Prosecution. Absent from the Defence teams, I notice Mr. Sarapa and Mr. Ostojic. Okay. Any preliminaries? None. Mr. Haynes, we had promised to come back to you on the break that you had asked for at the end of the -- your client's testimony. We've put everything in the basket when making our considerations and we have come to the conclusions that three days should suffice; however, in view of that, we are also authorising you to have access to your client in the meantime, provided that you restrict these approaches solely on the matters relating to the rest of the witnesses that you may or may not decide to bring forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. That's really very helpful. I won't bring any witnesses next week because I think given the technical problems yesterday, it's likely that Mr. Pandurevic's evidence will occupy a day or two of next week and that will then leave probably Wednesday, Thursday, Friday conveniently for us to regroup.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thanks very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we can continue with your cross-examination, Mr. McCloskey. Good morning to you, Mr. Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think you had mentioned, and I agree, that sometimes it's easier for lawyers to stand here and talk about things after the fact, like the Geneva Conventions. So I looked for something from a soldier and I found the values and standards of the British Army by the chief of the British General Staff Richard Dannatt, who you, I know, will have recalled reading his testimony in the Krstic trial. I want to go over a couple of those with you and get your views. This is a document that is short, relatively short. We've just got some excerpts from it. It is dated January 2008 and if we could go to the forward by General Dannatt which is page 3 of the English, and we did manage to get this part translated into B/C/S. It is 4307. I think as it's coming up, I can begin but as I said, it's entitled, "Values and standards of the British Army." The forward begins: "The British Army has a worldwide reputation for excellence, a strong reflection of its soldiers and officers. This reputation derives from and depends upon unequivocal commitment, self sacrifice and mutual trust. Our values and standards are vital to operational effectiveness. They are the life-blood that sustains the army. They have to be more than just words. We must believe in them and live by them. Therefore, it is the effective and coherent translation of these values and standards into actions that must penetrate every command and organisation until they are instinctive." And as you will recall, these are words from a man with combat experience in Northern Ireland where Catholics and Protestants were killing each other, in the Middle East and other places. He goes on to say: "Commanders create their command ethos," now we've translated that roughly to ethical environment. "Commanders create their command ethos and must ensure that values and standards are at the centre of it, through personal example and by educating and training their subordinates." Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with the way things are in the British Army and there would be no one happier than me if things were the same way in the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you, as a brigade commander in the Army of Republika Srpska, have responsibility for the command ethos of your unit?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every officer, which includes me as well, bears a certain responsibility as a human being and as a commander I -- an officer. And when it comes to the standards and values, here I found a sentence which says that the responsibility of a military officer, a professional, is similar to the responsibility of every citizen and above and beyond that. So the responsibility of a commander is important not only for its unit. What matters is also his behaviour and his actions in relation to the entire community in which he acts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it goes on to say: "The responsibility of commanders to be at the heart of this process cannot be delegated, and I hold you all accountable for it." Did you ever hear words like that from General Krstic or General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear those words but I have to tell you this, as a member of the JNA, I had the rules of service which indirectly rather than directly regulated the standards and behaviour of the JNA. However, there was no specific document similar to the one that you are showing to us now that would explicitly display and show standards and values that all the members of the army must adhere to. I would also like to say that these are the standard values of the British Royal Army whose tradition spans hundreds of years; whereas the Army of Republika Srpska was created during the chaotic times of war and its tradition is only four or five years long. Maybe this army will be in a position to issue a document similar to this in 50 or 60 years, maybe it will have different standards, very specifically explained. I would be very happy, as a soldier, to be able to serve in an army like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, I won't go over with you the guidelines that came out of the military prosecutor's office of the VRS that sound actually very similar to this and reflect the Geneva Conventions. But let me go on: "The values are about character and spirit: The standards define our actions and behaviour." Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It goes on: "I expect everyone in the army to abide by these values and standards."

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is expected, and as far as I can understand, this was issued in January 2008 but I believe that something of that nature existed even before. And I suppose that people did not adhere to the previous standards and that's why new standards had to be issued. You remember what the British soldiers did in Iraq, some individuals who did not adhere to these standards and their behaviour was even extreme although they were professionals. A commander can always expect and demand and whether his expectations and demands will be met depends largely on the overall functioning of an institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So are you suggesting that the fault lies in the soldiers and not in the commanders?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not suggesting that. I'm not suggesting that the fault lies in the soldiers. The fault lies in the organisation and functioning of a system or an institution. It is questionable whether these standards and values can be applied fully. We saw that the British Army was not able to fully implement its own standards when it came to its soldiers in Iraq.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you'll agree with me that all we can really do is try.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's see if the VRS tried. Let's go next to B/C/S page 4, this is under the section entitled "Values and Standards" under the operational imperative. And I want to read you paragraph 5 and ask you about it. "Soldiers are required to close with the enemy, possibly in the midst of innocent bystanders, and fight and to continue operating in the face of mortal danger. This is a group activity, at all scales of effort and intensities. Soldiers are part of a team, and the effectiveness of that team depends on each individual playing his or her part to the full. Success" -- and this is the part I want to ask you about. "Success depends above all else on good morale, which is the spirit that enables soldiers to triumph other adversity, morale linked to and reinforced by discipline." Do you agree that morale is extremely important?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you absolutely but I must add this, morale is not an abstract category. What you have just listed, all these things have an impact on morale. The first thing is professionalism and level of education of every individual, his personal courage, the attitude of the others towards him and vice versa and you can see here that it says that people function as a team. It's very difficult to compose a team of different people, different soldiers, in terms of their professionalism, age, education level and so on and so forth. It's not an accident that it takes at least four years of education for all who bear the same helmet on their heads to be thinking the same way when it comes to all of the issues that you've listed for us here. Every commander would very much like to have a -- his unit functioning as a team. This is theory. In practice, things are different, but I do agree with the wording of this document. I would word the document the same way myself. It is an entirely different issue as to how I would achieve the effect described in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sure General Washington would agree with you but his farmers were able to beat General Dannatt's army, the same farmers you had; but I don't think we need to get into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I don't think General Washington and General Dannatt were alive at the same time but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We don't need to comment on this any further. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to a document, 65 ter 4237, page 1 in the English, page 1 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, this is a document from the command of the Zvornik Brigade on February 10th, 1993, in your name and it's a report -- it's a regular combat report to the command of the Drina Corps. And if we could look at that first page, it's that first paragraph we see that: "At 1210 hours, the enemy artillery fired two H-122 millimetre shells in the immediate vicinity of the hospital in Simo Peric Street in Srpska Varos sector. A five-year-old child was killed, two civilians wounded and two houses damaged." These are Serb children killed by Muslim artillery fired into a city. How does this kind of conduct affect the morale of the troops on the line, the Serb troops?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since you've mentioned Washington, allow me to say just one sentence. Washington's doctrine says that diletants cannot wage a war and that soldiers to whom issues are -- orders are issued once a week or once a month can never maintain the same discipline as those who are issued orders every day. And now as to the document that you've just shown. This was a war which involved two warring parties but not two different states, but two different ethnic groups. This was a civil war with additional ingredients of a religious war. And if things like this happen on one side, the other side reacts impossibly and emotionally, and all the standards that exist are not taken rationally. Sometimes people react irrationally. This has a negative impact on morale of one's own forces. However, in my view, morale is not only the attitude towards one's self and one's own forces, morale is a component that also implies one's attitude towards their enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to another document, 65 ter 4313, dated 11 February 1993. It's the next day and I just simply want to point out what you say on paragraph 5, it's page 1 of the B/C/S, page 2 of the English, number 5. You say: "The situation in the area after yesterday's shelling of Zvornik and the industrial zone of Karakaj, the population is afraid of the attack being repeated with even more tragic consequences." So this, too, again affects the morale badly for the troops in the trenches, I take it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this does affect the morale of the troops in the trenches but also the mood of the entire society from which the soldiers hail and which the soldiers return after having spent some time in the trenches. This is very different from the situation of the troops who are engaged in combat thousands of kilometres away from their own home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. On this same subject, let's go to another document, 65 ter 4312. This one is from the Drina Corps command, dated 19 November 1992. It's from, you'll see, General Zivanovic and because it's a couple of pages, let me hand this to you. This is about an area we'll get into a little more deeper later but it's talking about the situation Cerska, at Konjevic Polje, Glodjansko Brdo, Kamenica, Snagovo. And the second paragraph says: "In addition to armed soldiers, there are a certain number of civilians (women, children, the elderly and the frail)," this is page 1 of the B/C/S, "in this area. We estimate this figure to be between 10.000 and 20.000 people." Then it goes on and talks about what the enemy is armed with. Then the next paragraph says: "The morale of the civilians is dropping due to shortages of food staples and other vital supplies. We deem that we will crash enemy resistance in a powerful attack precisely because of their drop in morale caused by joint attacks from all directions." So this is a situation where the VRS is coordinating their attack based on the falling morale or taking advantage of the falling morale of the Muslims; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is an estimate expressed here that the action will be successful, thanks to that. Morale means somebody's readiness to wage war and to engage in combat in war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So if you can crush the enemy's morale, you've got a better chance to beat them.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in principle, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And there's different ways of crushing the morale of the other side, isn't there? We'll get into some of those.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are different ways. I saw that you put on the list of documents the skill of warfare where the author says the best commander is the one who wins a battle without engaging in battle. That could be an answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think you mean -- well, translation that's the art of war, which I was going to go over yesterday but we kind of got into it a little quickly. Okay. Now, I want to go back to the values of the British Army again, back to 65 ter 4307. This comes under the chapter "Values." It goes through some values. On page 9 is where they begin with selfless commitment. Then on page 10, that's the English, and we have a translation of part of that, page 4 in the B/C/S, it describes courage. And I want to read this one to you: "All soldiers must be prepared to use lethal force to fight: To take the lives of others, and knowingly to risk their own. They may need to show restraint, even when doing so involves personal danger. They may witness the injury or death of their comrades but still continue with the task at hand. This requires physical courage, and soldiers will depend on each other for it." I don't think anyone here is doubting your physical courage. Then it goes on: "Moral courage is equally important. That is the courage to do what is right even when it may be unpopular, or risk ridicule or danger, and to insist on maintaining the highest standards of decency and behaviour at all times." Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. That's how it's written in the British Army and they probably adhere to that for the most part but I'm not sure that they adhere to it in full.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, human beings don't adhere to anything in full, we can agree on that. But let me ask you: Do you agree that moral courage is equally important as physical courage in battle, and after battle?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may be even more important than physical courage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It goes on and says: "This earns respect and fosters trust. Courage, both physical and moral, creates the strength upon which fighting spirit and success on operations depend. It is a quality needed by every soldier, but it is especially important for those placed in positions of authority, because others will depend on their lead and respond to it." When Dragan Obrenovic received the order relayed to him by Drago Nikolic, and he decided to provide Drago Nikolic with the commander of the MPs and some MPs, was he showing moral courage?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as we are comparing values and standards of one army with the behaviour of another army which two things are completely different, but still we are talking about some general standards and I believe the comparison possible. However, what Dragan Obrenovic told us Drago Nikolic required from him did not indicate that a crime was involved which would have required moral courage on the part of the first. But if you allow me to say this, if you compare the British Army, which is a member of the NATO alliance and very close to the American Army, in the bombing campaign against Yugoslavia, General Short of the NATO alliance said that everything needs to be done so that people do not have electricity in their refrigerators, gas in their heating appliances, that they cannot get to work. And the British pilots who bombed the bridges knew this. They were aware of this, so I wonder how this compares, how this fits in with the values and standards of that army and how they acted in conformity with --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, we can talk about what the allies did to Dresden as well but that's not my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to refer to page 12, lines 5 to 7, which is the initial part of the question posed by my colleague to the witness and it reads as follows: "When Dragan Obrenovic received the order and relayed to him by Drago Nikolic, and he decided to provide Drago Nikolic with the commander of the MPs and some MPs, was he showing moral courage?" Mr. President, this is a highly debated issue in this case. If my colleague is going to put a proposition to the witness, he can say, "If Dragan Obrenovic said something," or he can say, "It is my proposition that Dragan Obrenovic said something," but to make it as a statement that it happened like this is inappropriate. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's not inappropriate when I say it like that. It's what I mean my position is, that's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that's possible. The understanding is actually that it is a proposition that he is making and not a statement. I mean Mr. McCloskey is not testifying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, if you're not going to answer the question about Dragan Obrenovic, let me put it to you another way. If General Mladic ordered General Krstic to kill all the prisoners they could get from Srebrenica, it would have taken quite a bit of moral courage for Krstic to say no, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree completely. Not only moral courage, but also common sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I want to talk a little bit about some documents you spoke of in the context of command ethos. Could we go to 65 ter 2920. This is a three-page document, so unless I can get leave of Court to just hand you documents which may be easier --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I was going to make that point. It's really far simpler for the document to go directly from Mr. McCloskey to the witness than cause Eva to ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's do that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, General, let me give you the original.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, this is this document, 25 April 1995, you went over briefly with Mr. Haynes. And I'm curious, you testified that you had only glanced at it before signing it; right?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if that's what I said, all right, maybe I just glanced through it and signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, which was it? You testified about this.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've been testifying for 17 or 18 days. I believe I glanced at it and signed it. It's very difficult to quote from myself 17 days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to do that. I want to know how you were able to know all these years later that you just glanced at this before signing.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was the practice more or less concerning some documents that do not relate to combat activities themselves, but instead relate to briefs and reports like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who is responsible for sending the message in this document to the troops?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was drafted by the moral guidance organ; I signed it. It was sent to the command of the Drina Corps, probably also to other units of the Zvornik Brigade, and then the moral guidance organs from the brigade, through assistance for moral guidance in companies would pass the information on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who bears principal responsibility for in the brigade for this message sent to the troops?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The organ for moral guidance deals with these issues and I believe within the command they did not inform anyone in particular because the organs of the command were more or less involved in combat activities and knew what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who bears principal responsibility for the message sent out by this document in the brigade, you or Nenad, is it Nenad Simic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you at the beginning of my examination-in-chief, the commander of the brigade and the commander of the unit is responsible for elements of combat readiness. That's why he has assistants and associates through whom he can achieve that. Since my signature is here, I am responsible. I would be responsible even without my signature, not directly, but my responsibility for this document exists nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You are principally responsible for the message sent to the troops; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander is responsible in principle, as you said, and I was responsible for the overall situation in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this certainly wasn't the only document of this ilk that went out to your troops, was it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All sorts of documents are sent, reports, orders, pieces of information coming from superior commands, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's not my question. My question is: This is not the only document of this ilk, talking about the Muslims as "poturices," that came out of your brigade, is it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a report and we see that it's the 88th report in line; so it's not the only document, it's the 88th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was this kind of message organised from the Main Staff through the corps to the brigades?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is such a thing as internal information exchange within the army, it can go from the Main Staff through the corps to lower levels. There are also information exchanges at every level of the command. From time to time, we, as a brigade, received information from the corps that had been received by the corps from the Main Staff. Sometimes they would pass the information verbatim to lower units and sometimes we would use their reports as a basis for drafting our own message and sending it to lower units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, I'm not asking you about the process. I think we should be, if we're not, all experts in that process by this point. What I'm asking you is this: Was this message of demeaning the Muslims, was that a message that was organized by the morale folks of the Main Staff through the corps down through the brigades and then initiated by the commanders by their signatures? And I will remind you of General Gvero's opus entitled, "A Silk Cord for Alija," which I don't want to see on the screen.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There have been documents both from the Main Staff and the Drina Corps using such language, the same language as in this document. Almost none at the beginning of the war in 1992 and 1993, but in the second half of the war, that terminology was used more frequently in documents of the Main Staff, in the documents of the Drina Corps, and in the documents of brigades. And I can even explain why.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, I think you did and I'll ask you about that a little later. But let's go to another document, 65 ter 4256, it's page -- it's actually a one-page document and I have a -- again, I've got the original which I'll hand to you. This one, interestingly, is from the command of the Zvornik Brigade IKM, dated 3 April 1995. I guess a bit before the last one. I don't really want to get into the substance of it, but I see that the word "poturice" is used about 14 times.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I take your word for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So do you bear responsibility for sending this to the troops?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what effect does this message demeaning the Muslim people have on your troops?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No particular effect because that word has existed among the Serbs in Bosnia for centuries. It's not a new word and it's not a word they learned from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 ter 4282. This is a document from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, under the name of -- I believe it's General Milovanovic, and I have a -- our best copy, not great. I'm really mostly concerned about paragraph 2 where it says: "The Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska has decided by engaging the forces of the Drina Corps, 1st and 2nd Birac Brigades, and the Zvornik Brigade, the eastern Bosnia Corps, Semberija Majevica Brigades, at all costs needs areas to settle Islamic people with Islamic roots. The Muslims who are now in this area do not have Islamic roots. They are in fact poturice and were created from other peoples because they displayed cowardice in the face of the Ottoman invasion after the battle of Kosovo." So is this the meaning of the word that you said had been around for a long time as it is understood by the troops and yourself?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see every war that had been waged in the Balkans, especially in Bosnia and Serbia was a continuation of some previous war, even the wars from the times of the Ottoman Empire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm not asking about the history.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, we object to this question, Your Honour. My learned friend produces a new document which is purportedly authored by someone the Prosecution called as a witness in this case. They did not ask that witness about it, and now out of the blue, they choose to ask one of the accused about it. That is improper prosecuting, in our submission, and the Trial Chamber should not allow the Prosecution to use this document in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse. Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, also he's asked him what "poturice" means. He's about to tell him. He can't cut him off in the answer. And so either he can't tell him or he can tell him in his own words. He can't tell him in the terms Mr. McCloskey wants to tell him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Haynes. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, the "poturice" document was used at length by Mr. Haynes. The meaning of the word became at issue. In fact, I seem to recall you looking it up on the internet, and so we began looking at the documents to see if we could find a meaning and we did, and so in response to that, is what these questions are about. And I don't mind hearing the General out but if we could abbreviate the history lesson, I think it would be important except as it has the meaning to the word, I guess we can hear the history but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, our position is that we believe we take this to be a follow-up on what was asked earlier on during the examination-in-chief on the term "poturice" so please go ahead. In other words, Mr. Pandurevic, you need to answer the question; however, if possible, go straight to the point rather than giving a historical expose.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I've lost track of the question by now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't blame you. Let me take you there. You were told by Mr. McCloskey -- he read part of this document. Basically, I'll repeat the last part: "The Muslims who are now in this area do not have Islamic roots. They are in fact poturice and were created from other peoples because they displayed cowardice in the face of the Ottoman invasion after the battle of Kosovo." So is this the meaning of the word that you said had been around a long time as it is understood by troops and yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, that word dates back to that historical context and historians could give us a final judgement whether this is entirely true or not, but that word was well-known among the Muslims as among the Serbs. Like the word "Chetnik" has certain historical connotations for Muslims, the word "poturice" has certain historical connotations for Serbs. I don't want to go into broad historical explanations, although I am familiar with it, but I'm not the kind of person who goes into anyone's ethnic origins and counts their red blood cells.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to another document, 65 ter 333, it's from the command of the Zvornik Brigade. It's dated 18 July 1995. It talks about Muslims, as you'll see from the page 1, as "enraged criminal hoards of Srebrenica Turks." Going down to the fourth paragraph: "The brigade clashed with criminals arisen vampire-like with enraged beasts." So we've got the enraged criminal hoard, the vampire-like enraged beast, we have poturice. You are responsible for the message being sent to the troops demeaning the Muslims; correct? This document as well?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am, but this document speaks not of the Muslim people but the people I was fighting. You have to understand that in that war, we killed each other and that mutual hatred existed. Even today, things have not advanced much in Bosnia since 1992. But allow me to give an explanation about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: About what?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why these words started to be used more often in 1994 and 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We'll get to that very soon. But how is a soldier that receives something like this going to distinguish "poturice"? "Poturice" are cowards that couldn't withstand Islam, women and men, how is this soldier going to determine that you're just talking about the enemy here?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They knew from experience, the experience they gained during the war and that's why I wanted to provide a somewhat lengthy explanation and I will kindly ask the Trial Chamber to allow me to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm getting to that topic right now, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, but let him explain. Let him explain and then if you want to add or deal with other matters, you will be free to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have the beginning of his explanation on direct right here and perhaps it would save us some time if I could read that back to him and then he could go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead and then we'll see but we don't intend to restrict the General.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In regard to the first "poturice" document, Mr. Haynes asked you on page 30.835: "Were such words always used in documents of the brigade during the war?" You say: "No, they were not used throughout the war or rather from its beginning. At one point in the war, they creeped into our documents. I don't know exactly what that happened. You can see in the documents themselves. In any case, it was in 1992 and the forward as and the most part of 1993 when the word 'enemy' was used. I even found some reports dating back to November 1992 where it -- where in one of the reports, it says "the blue," and that was the word that we used in the staff military games and peacetime. The enemy was always represented as blue and our own forces were red. And that was the colours that we used on our combat maps. "Six months into the war, some people were still not aware of the reality of the situation. They were not aware that the war was really going on. But as the war continued, as the casualties mounted, the anger and hatred also mounted and those words assumed a different meaning and gained prominence." Further explanation, General.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. We obviously understand each other very well. We know what we want to say. As the war progressed, certain circumstances among the warring parties changed, accordingly, every side evaluates the morale of the enemy side. And within this process to evaluate the morale of the enemy, and in this case it was the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and its Supreme Command, we started from starting their ideological and political fundaments on -- from which the war campaign was launched. We started studying their war goals, their traditions that they relied on during the war and we also studied their behaviour and attitude towards the be enemy, i.e., us and the civilians. What we concluded was this: The basic goal of the political leadership of the Muslim element in Bosnia and Herzegovina was to achieve a unitarian Bosnia and Herzegovina with the prevalent Muslim influence and their ideological foundation was the Islamic declaration written by Alija Izetbegovic containing of two things, the Islamic society and the Islamic authority which excludes anything else. We knew that their main traditions were contained in Mehmet Fatih, the Osmanli conquerer who conquered Bosnia and Herzegovina. We knew what crimes were committed against the civilian population, particularly in the area of Podrinje, and that's why we started using terms that did not apply to the entire Muslim population because the entire population did not partake in the political view of Alija Izetbegovic. I apologise for this lengthy explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you say, "As casualties mounted, the anger and hatred also mounted and those words assumed a different meaning and gained a prominence," Dragan Obrenovic said very similar words to the Trial Chamber at his sentencing hearing. And I want to read those words back to you and ask you if you think they are similar. Prior to being sentenced and facing a potential life sentence, he got up and said these words at his sentencing hearing. 65 ter 4308. Among other things he said: "It was normal for every man, every male child to put on a uniform, take up a weapon, and to go protect his homeland, his nation. And ultimately his family. This was expected of him. This was his role, a sacred role. There was no choice. You could be either a soldier or a traitor. At the beginning of the war, it seemed as if the war and all it brought with it was impossible, that this wasn't really happening to us, and that everything would be resolved within a few days and that finally our generation would have a chance. We didn't even notice how we were drawn into the vortex of inter-ethnic hatred and how neighbours were no longer able to live beside each other, how death moved into the vicinity, and we didn't even notice that we had gotten used to it. Death became our reality. Unfortunately, it became everyday reality." It goes on: "Who, before that, could have believed the horrors of war would have become everyday reality? Who could have believed that they could become a part of our lives? Surrounded with horrors, we got used to them and went on living like that. Among those horrors, things happened that were done by people who knew each other, people who, until yesterday, had lived almost as family members together. In Bosnia, a neighbour means more than a relative. In Bosnia, having coffee with your neighbour is a ritual, and this is what we trampled on and forgot. We lost ourselves in hatred and brutality. And in this vortex of terrible misfortune, the horror, the horror of Srebrenica happened." Is he talking, before he faces his judgement, to the Court when he says about his hatred, is that the same hatred that you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is talking about the hatred that was created during the war and he is talking about the hatred having mounted during the war. It always takes two to tango in love and hate but I'm not sure that there's always a causal effect between the hatred and intention for one to commit a crime of such proportions as was committed after the fall of Srebrenica. I know that when I was in Slovenia, my cadets whom I had educated, shot at me. They tied an officer who was their commander and they tortured him. I didn't understand where that kind of hatred came from. I am quite appreciative of where the hatred in Bosnia and Herzegovina came from. Nobody who wasn't born there can understand that. It's just a sad fact but it's a fact. Life in Bosnia and Herzegovina, everyday life is deeply embedded in its history.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He goes on to say something else that I think responds to something you were testifying about. Right after he says: "We lost ourselves in hatred and brutality. And in this vortex of terrible misfortune and horror, the horror of Srebrenica happened." He says: "I am here before Your Honours because I wish to express my remorse. I have thought for a long time and I'm always followed by the same thought, guilt. I find it very hard to say this truth. I am to blame for everything I did at that time. I am trying to erase all this and to be what I was not at that time. I am also to blame for what I did not do, for not trying to protect those prisoners, regardless of my temporary nature of my then post. I asked myself again and again, What could I have done that I didn't do? Thousands of innocent victims perished. Graves remain behind, refugees, general destruction and misfortune and misery. I bear part of the responsibility for this." Do you question his acknowledgment of guilt and responsibility still?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, before I say anything else, I would like to say this: I did not lose my head the way Dragan Obrenovic did. I knew to separate to the good from the bad and I don't agree with him that it is hard to tell the truth. Telling the truth is the easiest thing to do; it's difficult to say a lie. Since he pleaded guilty and he was awaiting sentencing, I see this as a repentance. It was just begging for mercy. If he is guilty, he knows that he is guilty, but all that time he was telling me that he wasn't guilty. I don't intend to take the role of a Trial Chamber. If he says he's guilty then I suppose he is, but he may have been misled in legal terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You think it's his lawyer's fault?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I really cannot dwell upon the process that he had to go through and I can't be the judge of his moves and say why he did what he did, why he acted the way he did. But it is obvious that he had his reasons to do what he did and I'm sure that he did it of his own will, at least that's how the whole situation is represented in all of the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If you accepted the orders to kill the prisoners at Rocevic and Branjevo and allowed the Bratunac Brigade -- excuse me, the Zvornik Brigade, working with some elements of the Bratunac Brigade and others, to continue to kill people on the 15th and 16th, you would be just as responsible and guilty as he would; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I had ordered, approved, supported or in any other way contributed to the commission of a crime, I would be responsible and guilty. Whether he did all these things, I don't know. I've just learned based on what you have just read out to me, because one cannot glean that from his statement about facts. If he did all of this, then, yes, he is guilty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You have explained to us that you expected complete and truthful information from him upon your return. Can you explain to this Court why on earth, upon your return, Dragan Obrenovic would keep from you the fact that thousands of men had been killed and buried very close to your brigade, that thousands more remained in schools and had to be killed and buried. When you were facing what you were facing, why on earth would a military subordinate trusted and respected by you not tell you what you needed to know?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say why he didn't do that at that moment. It is even less understandable to me why he did not explain that in his statement of facts and in his interview in June 2003. When he was talking about these events, he only said one sentence. Allegedly he had reported to me that Jokic had said that people were being taken left, right and centre and were being killed. He never mentioned the name of a school, the number of prisoners, nothing concrete. He never explained that. Everything remained up in the air. What he told me on the 16th, in the evening and later on, he said much more than he said and has been recorded in any of the documents that originate from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, General, it's easy to criticise Dragan Obrenovic but you didn't answer my question. Do you want to?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to answer, however, there are questions that cannot be answered in any way that makes sense. You told me why he didn't tell me. You spent hours and days talking to him. Maybe you were able to conclude why he didn't. Maybe he was involved. Maybe his hands were covered and that's why he didn't tell me but I can only speculate. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think it's break time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a 25-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I want to continue briefly on this area of -- the general area of command ethos and I want to talk to you briefly about the entry of the 23 July duty officers' notebook by Ljubo Bojanovic that referred to Skelani having two injured Turks, that they cut themselves with glass and there's a -- "I told them to kill them since Bratunac doesn't want to take them." I'll bring that back up so we can see it but I just wanted to go over a few of the documents that we believe are related to this so we can determine if there's any substance to these comments. If we could go to 65 ter 220, B/C/S page 25, should be page 1 in the English. And this is a -- the log, you may remember, it's the Bratunac MP log and it's dated 23-24 July. And it says --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If the English could go to 23-24 July. Sorry, page 21, in the English, should be 25 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in the Bratunac log it says: "During the day, six Muslims were brought in and are now in custody. Two other Muslims were brought later but they were sent back since when they were in detention in Skelani they had cut their throats with a bottle and were already bleeding heavily. They were sent back." So like the entry in the notebook of the Zvornik Brigade, we have the Bratunac MPs saying that they had sent back two Muslims that had cut themselves with glass. Now, if we could go to 65 ter 2096, and this is a document from the Republic of Serbia Ministry of the Interior, the Bajina Basta area, which I think we'll agree is in the area of Skelani. And it's basically informing other MUP organisations that on 23 July, they handed over the following persons to the Bratunac-Skelani branch of the MUP. On page 2 of the B/C/S, you'll see - and it's page 2 of the English as well - that at the bottom, the last two people, numbers 7 and 8, noted to be Salihovic and Delic, were handed over at Bajina Basta border crossing because they'd injured themselves in order to avoid extradition. So you would agree with me that it looks like from these documents that Salihovic and Delic were in Serbia, they cut themselves with glass in order to avoid being sent back to the RS. Isn't that what it looks like from these documents?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here that they were handed over at the Bajina Basta border crossing because they had injured themselves in order to avoid being returned. Now, it doesn't say who they were handed over to. I don't understand from this. They probably just injured themselves fully expecting that they would be accommodated somewhere in Bajina Basta, in a medical institution there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay let's go to 65 ter 3137. It should be page 1 in both, and this is a Ministry of Interior Secretariat in Uzice, another Serbian MUP organ. It starts with: "Ethnic Muslims who fled Srebrenica and illegally crossed from Republika Srpska into the FRY territory were handed over at Bajina Basta OUP at 1800 hours on 23 July. "The Bajina Basta OUP employees handed over the above persons to the employees of the RS Skelani SJB for further processing." So that speaks for itself. It names the two people we've seen before, Salihovic and Delic. Now, just to -- for the final picture, 65 ter 4386. When that comes up, you'll see that it's a name and phone number listing that we found from the Skelani MUP and that the commander of the MUP, Milo Bogdanovic, commander of the SJB there, had a phone number of 854-389 which is the same number we see in the duty officer notebook which I will go back to. And there's an additional document at 65 ter 4387 that lists other -- that same phone number for the Skelani MUP. So I -- let's go back to the original document now, 65 ter 377. That is the entry in the duty officers' notebook made by Mr. Bojanovic. Now, it's the Prosecution's position that on the -- it's page 178, and this is just a short blurb so it's probably easier to look at it on the screen, General. That phone number that we see in English, and now it's coming up on the screen, is the number from the Skelani MUP. So it's the position of the Prosecution that the Skelani MUP, for some reason, phoned the Zvornik Brigade and said that they had two injured Turks that had cut themselves with glass and that Bratunac didn't want to deal with them. Now, we can see from the Bratunac MPs that -- report that they did not want to deal with them and sent them back and that Bojanovic said, "I told them to kill them." Now, these two men are on the missing list and it's the Prosecution's position that they were murdered and that we see this note relaying what Bojanovic said, and I'll remind you briefly Bojanovic testified about this and said that he'd admit that he was carried away by emotion when he did it but that he didn't think it would have been carried out. Now, this is something that he felt confident enough to write in the duty officers' notebook, communicating to any that looked into this. Do you think, sir, you bear any responsibility for this kind of conduct on the part of your subordinate officers?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I give you a specific answer, you've made several claims here and showed a number of documents that were not easy to follow. From those documents, we see that six persons were turned over at the Ljubovija border crossing, 40 kilometres or so to the north of Bajina Basta and these two were turned over at the Bajina Basta border crossing. We see the same persons are concerned. Ljubo Bojanovic explained a bit differently during his testimony why he acted in this way, differently from what you said. These people were not killed, they were alive and it was said before if Ljubo wrote this, and I didn't know that he did, nobody from the Bratunac Brigade could have implemented this order because the relationship between the Zvornik and Bratunac Brigade is not one of subordination. I think this was written out of indignation and protest, something like why did you find me to deal with them? Ljubo is not that sort of person and I don't feel responsible for this entry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You feel no responsibility whatsoever for Ljubo Bojanovic telling the Skelani MUP to kill those two people?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey. Do you wish to proceed to your next question or do you wish --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's not a proper -- in my view, that's not a proper objection in cross-examination. Sometimes for emphasis, sometimes for clarity that's appropriate. Of course it's your decision not mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, the previous question ran to 60 lines and ultimately, I was waiting to see what the question was going to be after he'd reviewed five pieces of evidence and made a long speech, but the speech was: Do you feel any responsibility for that entry? And that's precisely the same question he's just asked. There's no different emphasis in it at all and the question was answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey, do you wish to comment further? Or will you leave it in our hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I can go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Let's proceed then with your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What do you think of that entry?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's stupid. If somebody wants to commit a crime, why would they write it down? There must be something wrong with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let me go on to something you said in your testimony on 27 January 2009. You said: "Sometime in November, an order was issued according to which the Gorazde Brigade was to be reorganised. It was also part of the tactical group but it was falling apart because the population had been expelled from Gorazde area and I was ordered to form that brigade to be commander of the Gorazde Brigade." So do you believe that the Serbian population was, in fact, expelled from Gorazde by the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not my opinion. They were expelled, it's a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And you believed it at the time, I take it.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You also said on 28th January, 2009. 090212, day 371, page 30.793: "And what was the apparent intention of your enemy? "A. The intention of the enemy was to link up the forces of the 2nd Corps on the north and north-west sides of Zvornik with the forces in Kamenica, Cerska and Konjevic Polje. In the second stage, they would have taken the area on the banks of the Drina River and they would -- they would have eliminated any form of the Serbian life in the eastern part of that area." Do you stand by that statement?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you believe at the time in -- I believe this was 1992 or 1993 -- 1993, that the Muslims would have eliminated any form of Serbian life in that area?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have also seen documents, Muslim orders from September 1992 where it says, Burn down Kravica village with all the hamlets, raze them to the ground. It's just one example.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So in 1993, with the building hatred of your enemy that you have clearly described and an enemy that you think is bent on expelling you and your people and making life impossible, you have to control yourself and your soldiers from responding in like kind; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to the extent possible under the circumstances because their families had suffered, been killed, or expelled. They weren't waging war in some other country, they were doing it in their own village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you give me one example of you punishing or disciplining a Serb soldier for abusing or destroying Muslim property or persons?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, there was destruction of property during combat, which is collateral damage in fighting, and as for information that an individual had done something improper, I had no such information, and during the war, I did not punish any soldiers for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Not once? And I'm talking about not just structures, but abuse of Muslim human beings.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are talking about it, is that what you're saying? Who is talking about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your answer appeared to only answer the part about abuse of structures. My question is: Did you ever punish or discipline any VRS soldier for abusing any Muslim person?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying I had no information to warrant something like that and I did not punish anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. On a lighter subject, in this answer, I want to try to sort out, there was a point where you were the commander of the Visegrad Brigade and then involved in the tactical group and then they started -- you -- developing the Gorazde Brigade and you had some involvement in that. Can you explain, first of all, where was your headquarters for the Visegrad Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In several locations, the location changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you describe the locations and approximately when they changed?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think at the beginning, it was in Stara Banja in Vilina Vlas, for a while it was in the secondary school building in town, and for a while it was in the primary school in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were you appointed the commander of the Gorazde Brigade at some point in 1992?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you change locations when that happened?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was in Vardiste which is some 20 kilometres from Visegrad, right next to the border with Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When did you change locations and become the commander of the Gorazde Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, before that, from end September I had been in a place called Rudo, some 50 kilometres to the south of Visegrad; and after that, in the beginning of November, I transferred to Vardiste.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, in the beginning of November, when you transferred to Vardiste, you took command of the formation -- or the forming of Gorazde Brigade. Did your responsibilities with the Visegrad Brigade cease?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the Visegrad Brigade was a different man at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And how about your responsibilities towards the tactical group? When you became commander of the Gorazde Brigade, did your responsibilities with this tactical group you've described change at all?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a way, yes, because I was no longer in Rudo and I no longer had with me the men who had been in the command of the tactical group, and I had no such influence on the tactical group as I had had before. Formally, I was still the commander of the tactical group but the focus of my activity was to establish the Gorazde Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And I'm not going to get into the events in Visegrad. I'd like to go north now with you to Zvornik. Can you describe to us what the Birac region is?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Birac area is a territory in the eastern part of Bosnia and Herzegovina that gets its name after a chain of mountains and I believe it comprises Vlasenica municipality and later Milici municipality which had not existed before the war, plus Sekovici municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that would include Cerska as well.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Cerska was in Vlasenica municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Cerska would be part of the Birac region?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, logically, if Vlasenica is a part and this is a part of Vlasenica, then that, too, is part of Birac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I want to now go to directive 4, 65 ter 29. And if we could get that up there and, General, we'll give you a copy of this. I see it, I think we've highlighted -- I hope it's the right section.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No difficulty with that. No problem with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, I'm -- I hope I'm not going to spend much time on this but I just -- as we know, this is a Main Staff document to the various corps and you've said you never saw this and -- but I still wanted to ask you some questions about it and as we flip through it, we get to -- on page 3 of the English and B/C/S, after the initial discussions about the Muslim army, we get to the part where General Mladic says: "I have decided the following ..." And then paragraph 5 gets the tasks of the units under that big section, and that's page 4 of the B/C/S, page 4 of the English. And then he goes down through the various corps. And he gives very short, brief synopses of what he expects from the corps and we get to the section that I think we're all familiar with, section D, the Drina Corps. And it says very simply on page, B/C/S, 11; page 5 of the English: "The Drina Corps, from its present positions, its main forces shall persistently defend Visegrad, the dam, Zvornik and the corridor while the rest of its forces in the wider Podrinje region shall exhaust the enemy, inflict the heaviest possible losses on him, and force him to leave the Birac, Zepa, and Gorazde areas together with the Muslim population. First, offer the able-bodied and armed men to surrender and if they resist, destroy them. After that, unblock and repair the Konjevic Polje-Zvornik road, make it fit for traffic, and stand by for intensive combat against infiltrated sabotage, terrorist, surprise and ambush attacks and paramilitary groups. Set up a command post in Vlasenica and a forward command post as decided by the corps commander." Now, we see that this is dated 19 November 1992, I think it was sent out a bit later, if I recall. Can you tell us where you were, if you remember the -- were you at Gorazde at that point or were you still at Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Vardiste at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And so this part about force -- attacking the enemy and forcing him to leave the Birac, Zepa and Gorazde areas would have some application to you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This part concerning Gorazde in a way is right, although that brigade had not yet been fully set up and ready for combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. But in the sense that it involves Gorazde and what it says there, that would be of interest to you since it's coming from General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that he sent it to me -- if he had sent it to me in this form, if I had seen it, I would have been interested. It certainly concerned the Drina Corps, and I believe that based on this directive, the Drina Corps issued their own order down the line to brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you get that one?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that I ever received that order. I have seen here that it had come to the Zvornik Brigade and I said it was probably in the archive of the brigade, but I did not have it, to the best of my recollection, although I later was involved in certain combat activities that followed from that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, going back to directive 4, this part that says: "... Exhaust the enemy, inflict the heaviest possible losses on him, and force him to leave the Birac, Zepa, Gorazde areas, together with the Muslim population." What do you think of this section that says, "together with the Muslim population?" "Force the enemy to leave together with the Muslim population"?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's too late, whatever I think about it. The person who wrote this wasn't thinking, it's obvious, because if he had been thinking, he wouldn't have written this. This is something that should not feature in a military order and the activities of units can target only enemy units, not the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So are you saying that forcing the -- that this targets the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the primary aim here is to defeat armed forces and to force them to leave the area and then the civilian population is to go with them. The first part is completely legitimate but forcing the civilians to leave the area is not. They have to be given the option of leaving or staying, if they wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So your training of the Geneva Conventions tells you that forcing the civilian populations of Birac, Zepa, and Gorazde is, in fact, a crime, an international war crime of sorts?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it's deliberate transfer of the population, then yes; but if the civilians are driven out of the area of combat activities for their own sake, then it's not contrary to the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If the civilians are driven out -- if the civilians are forced out of their homes for their own sake. How do you make that decision, General? Have you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not make that decision. It's the person who wrote this directive that wrote it. What they meant by it, I don't know. I suppose they meant that the population also should be made to leave the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So is this what - and I don't know who came up with this - is this what has been referred to in your view as ethnic cleansing, forcing the population from their homes?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Forcing the population to leave the area where they live is not in conformity with Geneva Conventions, and whoever used the term "ethnic cleansing," it's an even uglier term.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, General Mladic used the terms used here and he is the one that must bear responsibility for this document; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So that we can infer from this document that on this date it was General Mladic's intention to drive the Muslims from their homes in this region; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says here but I know something different, that there was a decision of the president of the republic from end 1992 that refugees and abandoned property are temporary phenomena accompanying the war which means that once normal life is restored, everyone can come back and get hold again of their property.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, perhaps if there's a document referring to the Muslim refugees as temporary phenomena, we can find it. But you have heard the evidence in this case and I -- perhaps you remember, I think it was from one of those sessions of the Assembly where President Karadzic gets up and says, I stood by or I was part of all the first directives, 1 through 7. And then he says, But 8 and 9, involving Krajina, when we lost Krajina, I had nothing to do with that. You remember that evidence?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who made that statement and where.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we'll dig it up, I know it's a lot to remember. Now let's go to 65 ter 4221. Sir, this is a document -- I know -- well, I hope, especially with our electrical break yesterday, you've had a chance to see some of these documents and sort them out. But we can see here on the 20th of November, we've got a document from the Main Staff by Mladic that is ordering all Drina Corps brigade commanders to come to some sort of a political seminar in Zvornik on 23 November. Now, to put this in date sequence, we see directive 4, dated 19 November, we see this order to come to this seminar, the 20th of November, and there's some documents about that seminar which I'm sure you looked at with interest. Can you tell us, did you go to that seminar?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I will tell you. It seems that yesterday was to my benefit, the electricity was on my side. I was at that seminar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, then it benefited all of us in that case, General, because it's the position of the Prosecution that the seminar of 23 November, three days after directive 4, to deal with the topics as we see here, could have certainly discussed directive 4. And what I'm referring to is this document we have: "Pursuant to the request of the Supreme Command of the Army of Republika Srpska, Radovan Karadzic and with a view to carrying out timely preparation and holding a military and political seminar at the level of the Drina Corps, I hereby order: Prepare, organise and hold a military and political seminar at the level of the Drina Corps on 23 November 1992, starting at 1000 hours in Zvornik." It will be attended by the following: Karadzic, members of the government of Republika Srpska, representatives of the Main Staff, the core corps command, commanders of the brigades of the Drina Corps and presidents of the municipalities. Then number 3: "For the seminar, the corps commander shall prepare an introductory report on the situation in the corps, combat operations being carried out and the tasks for the corps in the days ahead, as well as the possibilities of implementing the tasks received. The speech shall take no more than 20 minutes." I want to ask you if that happened or not, the speech, that is. So did this seminar occur and did they discuss what they talk about here in 3, the tasks to be carried out by the corps and the brigades?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, that seminar was indeed held and it was indeed to be expected that a seminar of that sort would be held. It was only 20 days after the establishment of the Drina Corps; you know that it was established on the 1st of November. You know that Mr. Butler in his report, in paragraph 1 in chapter 1 thereof, said why the Drina Corps had been established and what was the threat of the Muslim forces on mountain of Cerska, Konjevic Polje and other parts of the Srebrenica and Bratunac municipalities. And it was only logical for the supreme commander to talk to his subordinate, the corps commander to learn what the corps was, how it was established, and what was it capable of doing. That was the purpose of the seminar, and since the brigade commanders had five minutes each, five minutes is not a lot of time and we could say very little. I don't remember the directive number 4 was mentioned at that seminar; however, what was mentioned was the role of the corps in the Podrinje area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So I'm sure after looking at this material, you thought good and hard whether or not directive 4 was mentioned. Are you sure it wasn't mentioned, as you sit back today and think about it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a member of the Army of Republika Srpska, this was my first participation in a seminar or a meeting in the presence of other people than those from Gornja Podrinje, from the tactical group that I was a member of, and I really don't remember that the word "directive" was mentioned. It may have been mentioned but I don't remember. To my best recollection, General Mladic wasn't at that meeting but General Milovanovic was. I may be mistaken but that's how I remember things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 ter 4222. It's one page but it ... Now, this is a document that we came upon which basically looks like it sets out a timetable for the military and political seminar and it's a little synopsis of what -- who is going to speak and what they're going to speak about it and it's approved and according to the translation we have a "za," approved for Ratko Mladic; is that the way you see it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see General Milovanovic's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we see the first person scheduled to speak at this is Dr. Karadzic. Do you remember him speaking?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And he should have been fully aware of directive 4 at the time, shouldn't he have?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That directive was signed by General Mladic. Whether he informed President Karadzic about it, I don't know. The directive should have been signed by Karadzic, not by Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: My question was: President Karadzic should have been informed of this directive; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree. I would say it's so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And then we see they only gave Karadzic ten minutes. There's no way he spoke for ten minutes, is there? How long did he speak for, any idea?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't tell you. You know how politicians are, they go on forever sometimes, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Then we see the commander of the Drina Corps, Colonel at that time Zivanovic gets second billing and he is to talk about the situation, results, further task and capability of the Drina Corps. Now, I'm sure you will agree with me -- and I am sorry, Ms. Stewart has pointed out to me our translation has left out Milovanovic who had second billing. No, sorry, we've misread that again. It's M. Zivanovic, we did have that right. Sorry, General. Now -- you've got to correct me when I make mistakes like that, if you can. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We need Mr. Haynes' permission.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm not sure that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you recall, General, Colonel Zivanovic would clearly have been informed of directive 4 at that time; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He received the directive. I believe he read it as well. But that corps existed for only 20 days and he did not have many results. However, General Zivanovic has the tendency to speak a lot without saying much. He makes promises without delivering and then finding excuses. Now, if he ever hears me saying this, I apologise, but that's how things were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, we have a brand new corps and we've just seen from directive 4, a very simple directive, defeat the enemy in the Birac area and Gorazde and Zepa and force them and the civilian population out of the area. Very simple. Very straightforward. Very easy to understand. Clearly, in this seminar, he would have outlined something about those two objectives; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I admire your understanding of a military situation and I will be very glad if you think that I understand legal matters as much as you do military matters. This is logical what you're saying, however, my understanding is that the Drina Corps was not established to expel the Muslim population from the area. That corps had a strategic importance and value. If you look at the geo and strategic deployment of forces in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time, the characteristics of the territory, when the eastern part of Republika Srpska fell or if it had fallen, the Serbian people would be on the verge of extinction in the entire territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That's why it was important to establish the Drina Corps and to preserve the Serb population in the area. It was not its goal to expel the Muslim population from the area; that's not why the Drina Corps was ever established in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So if you had your druthers, you would take that wording out of directive 4 and we'd forget about it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in a position to do that. If I had been in a position, I would not have written it this way. I would not have done things had that way. However, the order that was sent to the -- by the -- the Drina Corps based on this directive, I saw the goals, the sentence in the -- in the introduction is indeed there but the Drina Corps set out goals that do not mention any expulsion of the population. You've seen the document. You have it and I'm sure you can understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
