utterances.text: We'll get there, General, because as you've just said that the language did not disappear, it carried on and we'll get to it. But I do want to get to an interesting document, 65 ter 4402. This is something that we -- this is a document NATO picked up in a search in 2005 from a Karadzic residence in Pale which investigators from the Karadzic team believe is Karadzic's notes of that seminar. You can see that it's dated 23/11/1992. It's entitled "Conference." Does that look like his handwriting to you, President Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw this document among the documents that you sent to me. I could not recognise the handwriting and I was wondering whose handwriting it was. It is possible that it is his. I'm not sure. I only saw his signature. I did not see his handwriting in a written text that often.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recall his aides that were there as well? It's page 41 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some people around him. I can see my name. That's what he put down, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We'll go through this. It says: "Drina Corps commander of the corps, chief of the Main Staff, Defence Minister Subotic, and General Gvero." Do you remember General Zivanovic being there?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you remember the chief of the Main Staff, Milovanovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember him. I don't remember anybody else from the Main Staff but I may be wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How about Minister Subotic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know the man at the time. He may have been there but then, at that time, I didn't know him. I didn't know his face.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then we see General Gvero. You remember General Gvero being there?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have mistaken him for General Milovanovic. If the president noted the presence of all those who were there, then I suppose that that must have been so. You have to understand that this was quite a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I understand. So we see as we saw in the little outline of the conference, General Zivanovic is first up and it says: "Assignments: 1, Vitinica, Sapna, Teocak. 2, Cerska. 3, Zepa. 4, Srebrenica. 5, Gorazde." That sounds a lot like directive 4, doesn't it? Cerska, Zepa, Srebrenica, and Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see these are the places that were covered by the Drina Corps and it was logical to point to some places from which one could expect the biggest threat of the Muslim forces. Vitinica, Teocak, Sapna is north-west of Zvornik and that's where the forces of the 2nd Corps were. There were also strong forces in Cerska and also in Zepa and Srebrenica. There was a division in Gorazde as well. Whether General Zivanovic mentioned these as major strongholds or the places of threat for the corps or whether he thought that those were the places that need to be liberated, both options are possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. If we go down this, we see the other brigade commander, sometimes he says something, sometimes he doesn't. We get to you. You speak after Kornjaca, apparently. That's page 2 in the English. And then we have Captain First Class Pandurevic. He's got Gorazde, 5th Plpbr, he's got that right but he doesn't say anything about what you say. Did you in fact speak?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that I didn't say anything much during the five minutes that would have left an impact. Maybe the president wasn't impressed with what I said and that's why he left that space blank.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But you did speak?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose I did say something about the establishment of the Gorazde Brigade and the stage it's in. I didn't have much more to say. All the other brigade commanders were there from the -- and they all spoke about the situation in their respective brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recall if you responded to General Zivanovic's talk?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean "respond"? How would I have been able to respond to his speech? He provided an introduction about the situation in the corps and as far as I can remember, I didn't say anything. There was not much to say in response to what he had said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me give you a hypothetical. Let's say Karadzic or Zivanovic before you outlined the objectives of the Drina Corps and from the only document laying that out that we know about, directive 4, let's say they said, The objective will be defeat the enemies in these areas and drive out the population. What would have happened to you if you had gotten up and said, Gentlemen, I will defeat the enemy all day long but I will not participate in driving out the population as you state. What would have happened to your career, had you said that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it would have had a major impact on my career. Maybe somebody would have reacted and said, You don't understand the situation. However, since it took me over two and a half hours to get from Zvornik -- Visegrad to Zvornik across Serbia and that the only road was Zvornik-Caparde-Sekovic-Han Pijesak-Sokolac, and that road was not safe, and since I did not know the terrain in the areas of Birac and Podrinje but I knew that the situation was critical in military terms, I really don't know that anybody spoke about the expulsion of the population but I know that a reference was made about securing roads and defending Podrinje. I'm absolutely sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 ter 3029. This is the document you have spoken of, the Drina Corps version of directive 4, dated 24 November, the day after this conference. This particular version is to the Zvornik Brigade and as we see, it cites the Main Staff number 02/3, 19 November 1992, which we'll all agree is directive 4. And it says number one: "Launch an attack using the main body of troops and major equipment to inflict on the enemy the highest possible losses, exhaust them, break them up or force them to surrender, and force the Muslim local population to abandon the area of Cerska, Zepa, Srebrenica, and Gorazde." So we see right after this conference, and we know this is General Zivanovic or Colonel Zivanovic, he's adding to directive 4. Directive 4 just said defeat the army and force them both out. He has a whole sentence just for the Muslim local populations, "force the Muslim population to abandon," he says "abandon," and then he lists specifically places in the Birac region, Cerska, and then goes on to list Zepa, Srebrenica, and Gorazde. This was not by accident that he wrote this down, was it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose this was not by accident. However, he referred to directive 4. He invoked it. And then he wrote what he did. And he determined the goals of the operation and the goals should have arisen from the tasks that were given at the beginning. The first task should have been the expulsion of the population from that area but that goal is not there, hence there is no tasks. So the goal is simply not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, I won't argue with you about what's there and what's not there. We see this statement. We can read that for ourselves and we'll continue to look at the documents and what happened on the ground to see if we can answer that question. Now, let's go to 65 ter 30. This is a Main Staff document dated 7 December 1992, entitled "Order to amend directive 4." To the commander personally. If we look at the end of this, we'll kind of cheat, we can see that he's basically sending it to all the corps commands including the Drina Corps. I think historically we know that December 7th, 1992, was at the peak of the Muslim army's attack in the area of Birac, Srebrenica, particularly Kravica was around this time as I'm sure you will agree, the VRS is suffering under that attack. And so with that background we can read the paragraph: "There is an organised campaign to provoke a confrontation between the military and civilian authorities in Republika Srpska. Meanwhile UNPROFOR forces are trying to incite conflicts between the Army of Republika Srpska and the Serbian people by bringing in humanitarian aid to Muslim settlements through the Serbian territories, demanding from the Army of Republika Srpska to ensure this, abusing the signed agreements on the obligation of warring parties to ensure the passage of humanitarian convoys." It goes on and talks about other things. And then it gets to the order: "That all targeted objectives of the Army of Republika Srpska must be achieved (reached) by 13 December 1992 at the latest." Then it goes on to describe that a little more. Then if we get to the next page in English, it starts with -- page 3 in the B/C/S, excuse me. "For this purpose, the goals and tasks set out in directive 4 of November 1992 are to be completed by that date." And then it says: "Despite the stages formerly set out in directive 4, the corps commands must carry out the following assignments in their zones of responsibility by 13 December 1992: Keep the lines achieved so far." Then number 2, liberate Orasje, Trnovo, and for us we see Konjevic Polje, Cerska and then Teocak. So will you agree with me that directive 4, as we read it, is alive and well on the 7th of December and the corps has been given a deadline by which to meet those objectives set out in directive 4?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Directive 4 never took off the ground that easily. It was drafted on the 19th of November and it was only sometime towards the end of January and the beginning of February that something more concrete was done pursuant to that directive. In my view, this was on the eve of some negotiations or maybe the end of the war was expected. Every side wants to take the best positions before the negotiations and this is where the corps were ordered what to do before the 13 December. This was impossible, it says liberate areas or places, not expel the population. War is a dynamic phenomena and the whole sense of a military is to fight, to occupy and keep certain territories, that's the whole point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: My question is, sir, according to this document which is telling the Drina Corps to follow directive 4 and meet its objectives, directive 4 is still alive, well, and active and -- and active.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, directive in itself is a document covering a longer period of time within which certain tasks have to be implemented, but some tasks from the directive were never implemented. Some were implemented in part and some in full.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now this dated 7 December, let's go to the next document, 65 ter 4279, which is December 8th, the next day. And this is from the Drina Corps and it's to the Birac, Zvornik, and the Bratunac and the Milici Brigades. Now, this is roughly what -- December 8th, is that about a week before you get to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ten days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we can see at the top, that this is -- it says, "Decision on the liberation of Pobudje, Konjevic Polje, and Cerska." And as we saw on the previous document, it talked about the liberation of Konjevic Polje and Cerska. So based on the date, the topic, the headings, we can infer, can't we, that this document sent to the brigades is a result of the Main Staff order of 7 July that we just saw?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 7th December. Yes, you're right. It's the military logic and that's what the documents say. You are right so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we go to page 3 in the B/C/S and page 3 in the English, we see that there is a job for the Zvornik Brigade. It's under section B, I think -- auxiliary forces. So do you agree with me that that -- I'm sorry, do you agree with me that that document of the 8th is based on the December 7th document previous to it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but let me tell you this as well, namely what all these previous documents are based on. They're all based on some decisions and intentions of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. There were two sides for the -- to the conflict. This is not just random making of moves, this is a conflict. This is warfare.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I agree with you and it's in fact true these documents are based on the original intentions of the supreme commander Radovan Karadzic and his commander of the Main Staff Ratko Mladic as set forth in the directive; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but why did they write it like that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I can't answer that one. All right. Let's go to 65 ter 4225. We're getting closer to your arrival. This is a document from the Drina Corps to the Zvornik Brigade and the 5th Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade and let me ... It's entitled, "Measures to be undertaken for the defence from the military intervention of foreign countries against Republika Srpska." Aside from -- and I believe this is General Zivanovic and some derogatory remarks about the Muslims and their sick imagination, he gets to the business of the order, finally, on page 2 of the English, page 2 of the B/C/S and says: "In order to mitigate potential attack of the aggressor against our forces and to break the power of the aggressor and of Muslim-Croatian forces I hereby order ..." The first point is: "Perform energetic actions to complete all the tasks referred to in order strictly confidential number 2-126 of 24 November 1992," and that is the number of directive 4. And "Decision for liberation of Pobudje, Konjevic Polje and Cerska strictly confidential number 2-198 of 8 December 1992." Did you receive this order, sir?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it did come to the brigade but I probably didn't see it later. I knew, however, the mission of the Zvornik Brigade. You see this is the fifth order after directive 4 requiring that some of these tasks be realised and it enumerates the places that have to be liberated. This is a chess-board on which Muslim forces make moves as well. Their mission was to get to the Drina as soon as possible and liberate certain areas. Our task, our job, was to defend ourselves from it and liberate other areas, but at this point, no one had done anything yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: My simple point is again we see the citation of directive 4 so directive 4 is still in operation, still being cited by 11 December 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. But it also shows something else, to what extent the Army of Republika Srpska was disorganised, too disorganised to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It wasn't too disorganised for you to be able to find out what directive 4 was so that you could understand this order, was it? This order was sent to you, it makes reference to directive 4, you could have or should have looked at directive 4; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not look at directive 4 because everything that came from the corps level or brigade level I saw and knew. Whether I was able to organise it is something different. This looks more like war games, that they could have ordered anything but it doesn't necessarily mean it was possible to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Shall we have the break now, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That would be great.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. For the record, Mr. Ostojic is now with us. Mr. McCloskey, you may proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just to clarify for the record, 65 ter 4225, the 11 December 1992 document from the Drina Corps that made reference on page 2 of strictly confidential 2-126, I think I had said that was directive 4, that is the Drina Corps version of directive 4 so just to clear that up. And if we could now go to 65 ter 4226.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We are now, General, into a time-frame where you were clearly at the Zvornik Brigade. This document goes to the Zvornik Brigade and it is from the Drina Corps command and you can see that the Zvornik Brigade is one of the first addresses but it -- with the rest of the -- some other brigades and then number one is -- just to double-check that it's Colonel Zivanovic writing this, number one says: "Due to the unfavourable balance of forces, corps units did not accomplish all tasks under decisions for further operations (strictly confidential number 2-126 of 23 November 1992) which the enemy took advantage of for a counter-attack in the eastern and southern sections of the corps zone of responsibility." Now, strictly confidential 2-126 23 is the Drina Corps version of directive 4 with that language we have spoken about. You would have received this, I'm sure, February 1st, this is after Naser Oric has done his work, and do you recall reading this?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that I received this order and I suppose I did read it at the time because I received such tasks and I'm aware of this task of the Zvornik Brigade but let me just say one thing. There are no variations of directive 4. Directive 4 is one and only and it gives rise to the tasks which are then elaborated by the various corps commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, I'll try not to refer to it as the Drina Corps version of directive 4 again but you know what I mean; right?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know. I don't know what you think about General Zivanovic who signed this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you agree with me that the language in the Drina Corps order that echos directive 4 order is just as criminal as the directive 4 original.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, not at all. I would not entirely agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, as we've gone over it, it's even more specific about forcing the population out -- I'm not talking about the one in front of us, I'll go back to the one that we were -- that you were scolding me about earlier, if you'd like.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the one that is before us and it was also signed by the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, let's go back to 3029 just to clarify this important point. Now, the document that I was talking about is the Drina Corps version of directive 4, which I won't do again, but what I was talking about is this document that we have on the screen, the 24 November document. It mentions, "force them to surrender," referring to the enemy, and then, "force the Muslim local population to abandon the area of Cerska, Zepa, Srebrenica, and Gorazde." That language that we see on the screen, you would agree, is just as criminal as the language from directive 4.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have already agreed on that, Mr. McCloskey, but I added to that that the goals and the operations in themselves are not criminal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go back to the one that we started with, 65 ter 4226, and we see that, as I'd said, it cites this document, the Drina Corps document of 24 November. You would have received this document, as you said, so did you go and find confidential 2-126 of 23 November so you could understand what this February 1 order is talking about?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember whether I saw this document or not, but I know that the corps command did issue me with a task to take the axis from Zvornik across the broader area of Kamenica and push the enemy further towards Glodjansko Brdo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, General, I asked that because, as we both agreed, the comments by General Zivanovic are obviously criminal, and had you gone back and looked at this I would have thought you would have remembered or perhaps not?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've told you what I've told you. It really doesn't matter whether I saw them then or whether I see them now. I told you what I think. The positions are criminal. You spoke to General Zivanovic and it -- I believe that he would be better suited to talk to you about this than I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to page 2 of the current document; it's page 2 in both versions. It talks about the situation and on the 4th paragraph down it says: "The civilian Muslim population is being evacuated via Kamenica," probably from Kamenica, Cerska and Konjevic Polje, "along the following route: Glodi village," then a bunch of other villages. And they say there's -- "According to the statement of a prisoner on 30 January 1993, around 2.000 civilians were prepared for evacuation." It then says: "According to information gathered, the enemy's morale has been rather shaken for the following reasons: Heavy losses; the loss of captured or previously held territory; a lack of ammunition and food; the impossibility of prompt delivery of humanitarian aid; and the impossibility of normal living conditions due to the constant firing of our artillery, especially in the current winter conditions." Is that how you remember it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that combat was going on and at some points they were more successful; at other times, we were. I can't remember the exact language but I received this paper at the time and I certainly read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it goes on to say that: "I have decided" -- this is the bottom of page 2 in the English. "A group main forces for the liberation of Cerska and Konjevic Polje and all auxiliary forces for the liberation of Kamenica." Then it gives the tasks of the specific units, I don't want to go into detail about that but you are given specific tasks and it appears you have two or three tanks from the first paragraph. That's page 3 in the B/C/S and it's paragraph 4.1, page 3 in the English. Do you also have artillery at your disposal?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the next document 65 ter 4227. This is a Drina Corps document to the Zvornik Brigade, and I just wanted you to take a look at -- it should be B/C/S page 1. Let me give you a -- English page 3. And it says: "In accordance with the assignments specified in directive 4 with addenda to the main forces of the Drina Corps are to continue conducting combat operations in the TG Visegrad and the operation aimed at liberating Srebrenica and Zepa ..." and it goes on to talk about that, in particular. And near the end of the document, it talks briefly about the Zvornik Brigade. So from this document, we see that directive 4 is still in action, so to speak; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree, it's still in force. It was in force for a long time and stage by stage, the tasks from that directive were implemented, but allow me to add this. The establishment of the Drina Corps would have been completely out of place if General Zivanovic had been sitting in Vlasenica and I in Zvornik. One morning we would have woken up to find the BH army in Zvornik and Vlasenica, respectively. This is quite logical that the corps should be doing what it was supposed to do when it was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's go to another document, 65 ter 5D01323 and this is a big document but I don't want to spend much time with it. It's dated September 15, 1993, from the Drina Corps by Zivanovic, and it's entitled, "The realisation of planned tasks from directives number 4 and 5." And I just want to ask you if you agree with the section that's in B/C/S page 9, English page 12. This, from my understanding, is just a kind of an after-action report kind of document, and paragraph 16, it says: "After regrouping the forces, the 1st Zvornik Brigade supported by the KAG ..." KAG, that's an artillery group or something else?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the corps artillery group.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: "Carried out an attack on the given axes and liberated the sector of Kamenica village, Glodi, Rasevo, and Konjevic Polje and then continued the attack towards Kravica." Is that right, roughly?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's true, completely true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then just that map that's behind you, I don't want to go into detail about it. That is a map that was -- and I'll get a 65 ter number for it -- that was entitled, I believe it was "Operation Proboj." Is that the area where these actions occurred, roughly?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the area more or less. But you could have looked at point 2 in this document, the objective and tasks of the operations and the time allocated. In contrast, it lasted for almost two and a half months and that tells us a lot about the operation. The operation is something that involves two or three or four brigades; that's a lot of soldiers. This is, in contrast, a string of unconnected operations and what you showed on the map corresponds to the Proboj operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that map is 4399. All right. Let's go to a document you referred briefly to in your direct, 7D1006, which is a one-page document but I'm sure you'll remember it. It's the one where you talk about a prisoner you've captured and you send them back with a message.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is 1 February 1993. And so to help put that in context, I would like to go to a document before that, 31st of January, 1993, 65 ter 4229, from the command of the Zvornik Brigade and you can hang on to both documents. This is a regular combat report in your name and it says in number one: "The enemy did not carry out any significant operations apart from occasional fire in individual parts of the front. However, large movements were observed overnight and today from the direction of Crni Vrh via Tisova Kosa and Pandurica where a column of about 200 women and children pulled out during the night and some of them went astray and froze." And then on the next page, in English page 2, it says that: "The situation in the territory, Radio Zvornik broadcasted a proclamation to the Muslim people, women and children, from the Cerska and Kamenica areas that they could leave the territory without hindrance. The brigade command is securing a corridor for movement and no repressive measures will be taken against people leaving the area of combat operations. The corridor will be opened on 2 February 1993 from 0700 to 1700 hours." It goes on to say that the increased rate of women, children, and elderly crossing from Kamenica sector through Snagovo and Crni Vrh towards Pandurica may be expected to continue. So is this what happened? You got together with the radio station and this got broadcast to the Muslims to facilitate their movement out of the area, some of them freezing to death in the process?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see this report is dated 31st January and it makes a reference to the people who went astray and got frozen, so they did not get astray and got frozen after the proclamation. The proclamation followed this event. Also, the area between Milici and Baljkovica was not held by the VRS until April 1993. It's an area that was subject to constant infiltration into Kamenica and Konjevic Polje areas and there was constant movement of the population from Kamenica, Konjevic Polje and Cerska. Muslims often organised the movements of this population themselves and provided escorts. When we received reliable information about these movements, these developments, I thought it would be only human to enable these people to go out of the area of combat without wandering around and getting lost and getting hurt. That's why this was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who decided to open this corridor?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Hold it because we --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could I kindly ask you to repeat from the beginning, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I can't remember exactly whether I came up with this proposal to open the corridor and then informed the corps and then all this was done with their consent or perhaps all this was done and then the corps was informed. If you have reports to the corps, maybe you can find it there. I'm not sure about the sequence of moves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I seem to recall your direct testimony that you said that you did this?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, if I said that, then it must be so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 ter 4232. I see we've done some highlighting but -- thank you. This is a Drina Corps document, February 1st, where if we just look at page 1 in the English under paragraph 3, we're now calling the Muslims: "The Ustasha leaders have felt that their inhabitants shall move out of Cerska-Srebrenica area and stop being their hostages. I decided to allow the inhabitants to move as they did still tomorrow on the 2nd of February, 1993, I am going to warn them through the media that the corridor is closing on 2 February 1993 at 5.00 p.m. It shall be possible to leave the territory for all people without exception and only with my permission." So is Zivanovic in control of this or are you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see my report went to General Zivanovic and he signed almost verbatim what I said in my report because my report says that I decided to send this prisoner in Kamenica and pass the information about the opening of the corridor. Zivanovic put that in his report and he wrote it in the first person as if that's something he had decided even before getting my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's look at 62 ter 4233. This appears to be dated 31 January, although there's some strange dates in the English version. It says from you --

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- to the command of the Drina Corps, report on unusual incident. "On 30 January 1993, at around 2400 hours, a mixed column made up of women, children and armed men from the direction of Udrc via Glodi," and other places, "and in the direction of Kalesija and Tuzla, fell into the ambush in Crni Vrh sector. The column, which numbered about 100 persons, was fired on and dispersed and disappeared from the sector of the fire and the ambush. All our units were at full combat readiness and no one was killed or wounded on our side." So what kind of weapons did you fire at these women and children and soldiers with, any artillery or just small arms?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see I said a moment ago what corridor that was and how both civilians and armed men passed through it. This was obviously a mixed column where the armed men protected the column of civilians going with them. The people who were setting up ambushes were probably unable to know whether all of them were armed or not. They opened fire. I cannot tell you whether they opened fire on armed men or on everybody; however, you do know that it's impossible to set an ambush with artillery. I found out about this, informed the corps, and then the next day, the order to open the corridor came.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So, General, are you suggesting that it's the men that conducted these -- this ambush that are the most responsible for this, firing on the women and children?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you're talking about opening fire on women and children. What the document says is that fire was opened on the column. If we interpret the regulations on international humanitarian law literally as written into the laws of the SFRY, then we see that this column contained armed men, and nobody can be held responsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So in your view, if there's 100 people and some armed men in there, you can fire on them no problem, even if there's women and children? Children, General?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, a document has to be read from beginning to end. It doesn't say, "a few armed men among women and children." It says "women, children, and armed men." And of course it's not the women and children who went to the head of the column; it's the armed men who headed the column. Women and children were never targets of my activities or fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did this ambush on the women and children and the soldiers increase the morale of your units?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ambush was not set for the women and children. Ambushes were set up to prevent break-throughs, infiltration of forces from Tuzla and the pull-out of forces from -- to Cerska. This day, this mixed column turned up. The ambush had not been set to boost morale because that section of the road where the ambushes were set was frequently where the Muslims set their ambushes. A lot of vehicles and a lot of civilians were killed by ambushes from Crni Vrh; that's why we set up counter-ambushes on our side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, my question was: Did this attack on women, children and soldiers, as described here, improve the morale of your unit?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it did not. These civilians were collateral damage. It's a modern term that arose, we all know when. They were not a deliberate target. This could only have weakened combat morale.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you know there were some collateral damage. How much? How many people? How many children?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say how many there were or that there were any. I'm just saying that if somebody is with the military column, they are a target. And it's not me who invented the term "collateral damage" for any injuries or killing that result from such situations. You know who came up with that term.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You said there was collateral damage. You were there. That's why I ask you who and how many?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't there. Maybe it's a misinterpretation. What I meant and what I said was that people can be considered collateral damage if they find themselves within a military column and if they are a legitimate target according to the regulations valid in the SFRY and the regulations that arise from international humanitarian law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's take a look at 65 ter 4234, another document dated 31 January. I'm sure you've seen this. It's a regular combat report under your name. It says, number one: "There was occasional enemy fire overnight during the passage of a column from Cerska through Udrc, Snagovo and Crni Vrh. During the afternoon, mixed columns made up of women, children and armed men were again seen moving from Cerska via Udrc, Glodi, Redzici, Snagovo, and Crni Vrh towards Kalesija and Tuzla." Then if we go over to page 2 in the English, paragraph 5: "The situation in the territory is somewhat more favourable following yesterday's scattering of enemy groups who were attempting to link up with the forces from ..." somewhere. Is that a reference to the ambush on the women and children and soldiers, or something else?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You probably understand it's something completely different. Look at the date of the report, 31st January. It's about a column noticed on the axis indicated here. And then on the 31st of January, it says the column broken up yesterday, not the one that was noticed but the enemy group that had attempted to link up with forces from Medjedja which means a military target.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's look at 65 ter 4253. This is dated 2 February 1993. This is, again, one of your reports and I'm mostly interested in the second page of the English, the first page of the B/C/S. It's number 8. "Given that a large number of civilians, women, children, and elderly people have pulled out of the Kamenica sector, it can be assumed that those who have stayed and are able-bodied, and at the same time hold extremist views, will continue intensified operations in order to link Kamenica-Snagovo-Kalesija." So do you think that the able-bodied men that stayed behind hold extremist views? Where does that come from? Because they want to guard their villages?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, from all that has been said so far, it turns out that I was an extremist and something like that can be ascribed to me. If we know what had happened by that time with Kravica and the 140 villages and hamlets in the area of Bratunac municipality, and if we are aware of all the other sacrifices and victims on the side of the Serbian population, then this is something quite understandable then in this report of the 2nd, we know that the civilians had passed through based on the proposal we had made to them. I don't see why this word is so controversial. Why is it bad to call someone who had committed such a heinous crime something like that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, I won't argue with you, General, but we all know that peoples don't liked being lumped together like that, that these are crimes of individuals we're talking about. You can't possibly suggest that the farmers that are part of the 28th Division that are guarding their homes in these areas, and their mosques, are some sort of extremists because they want to guard their homes and mosques, are you? Or are they all Naser Oric in your mind?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to 65 ter 4238.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I haven't answered yet. I started and only "no" was recorded, I'm sorry. Certainly not all of them were considered to be extremists; some of them were. A book was published sometime last year written by a man who had lived in Srebrenica at the time of Naser Oric and with whom he had been in conflict all the time. And he said at one point it was easier to survive Chetnik attacks than our own local balijas, "balijas," meaning the Muslims who terrorised their own people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So how many terrorists -- how many horrible balija terrorists were there, in your view, in Srebrenica in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. The author of the book, Ibran Mustafic, who wrote that book called, "A Planned Chaos," probably knows.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The hatred you talked about, General, is it still with you? Sounds like it.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you're not hearing very well or maybe your ears are too sensitive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Bringing up that kind of book and that kind of talk in this trial seems to me that you're doing it to vilify the Muslims, sir. Why else would you have said that? I'm talking about the farmers that are guarding their villages in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we try and keep a professional tone to this? This is very really very emotional from Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let him answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is precisely what I want to make a distinction between, those extremists and simple farmers who were defending their villages, and I understand this in the same way as you do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. General. Let's go to 65 ter 4238. It's an intercept between one person named Zivanovic and a person named Gaborovic, and it's page 2 in B/C/S. Let me give you the printout. We found a Gaborovic from the 5th Communications Battalion. Could this be General Zivanovic and Gaborovic from the 5th Communications Battalion or can't you tell?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose this is a conversation between General Zivanovic and Mr. Gaborovic who was in the 5th Communications Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah, we do see references to Captain Jevdjevic. And of course, as we go down through this intercept, we see that after some discussion, that Gaborovic says: "The valley below Mandici, down towards Rogosija, they used that space between and killed a man and wounded his wife, and then they took his cattle. The police should check that. I spoke to Captain Jevdjevic and there is a possibility that they continued towards Kladanj, that they are retreating so they use the cattle for demining and for food." Then Zivanovic says: "Catch up with them and fuck their mothers now." And then he says: "Understood?" Then Zivanovic says: "Hold tightly the positions ... are the Turks' houses burning?" He says: "They are burning, they are burning." "Way to go, as many as possible." Were Drina Corps forces burning Muslim houses around the period of February 8th, 1993?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this conversation they are talking about a Muslim group that had been infiltrated and carried out sabotage acts. This one is asking the other about this. The first one is asking whether the Muslim houses are burning and he says yes, yes. Some houses were burning. I know at Glodjansko Brdo, houses were not burned down and when the brigade passed through, the houses were not torched.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you don't know anything about what Zivanovic and Gaborovic were talking about here?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all I can see is that they are talking about the subject of their conversation and they are mentioning some houses that are on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to 65 ter 4235, it's dated 13 February. This is a report from your brigade in your name. To the command of the Drina Corps. Number one: "Apart from the usual enemy fire in the general area of the line of contact, in the Nezuk sector two groups of civilians and soldiers were sighted and fired on with artillery weapons."

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So did you fire on the civilians with artillery weapons like it says here?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have been this: At the front end of strengthening defence lines, some civilians were working and then fire was opened, whether it was opened only at civilians or at soldiers and civilians or alternatively only at soldiers, we can only speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We don't have to speculate because it says fire was opened on -- "two groups of civilians and soldiers were sighted and fired on with artillery weapons."

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What millimetre artillery would have been used in that context?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. Artillery had different calibres, whether those were --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you please slow down because the interpreters are finding difficulties. And repeat, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know, Your Honour. It's the 18th day. Even if I had won the Oscar, everybody would have been tired by now. I said we had different types of artillery weapons, mortars, 82, 120- and 76-millimetres, 105-millimetres, 122, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you take responsibility for the firing of artillery in this report?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 ter 4254, another report from you, General, 15 February 1993. Paragraph 3, in your name: "The success we achieved in the southern part of the front has been a morale booster for further combat operations to expel the enemy from centuries-old Serbian homes."

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So the Muslims were living in century-old Serbian homes?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the area shown on the map, you see a large number of Serb villages from which the Serbs had expelled been at the time and they had lived there for centuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You're talking about the Muslims from the Muslim villages, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here "expelled from Serb century-old houses." They were mixed Muslim and Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me show you a document, it's 65 ter 1499. It's something we found in the Drina Corps collection by General Krstic. It's a map that shows the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa -- I'm sorry. As you know it takes a while for maps to come up on this thing. And over the enclaves it has the symbol of the four Serbian Ss and it says next to Srebrenica with a date: "Srebrenica has been Serbian and remains Serbian." Can you read to us what it says about Zepa?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "And Zepa is Serbian too, 27 July 1995, Major-General Radoslav Krstic".

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Srebrenica is dated 12 July 1995. How is it that General Krstic considers Srebrenica to have been Serbian and remain Serbian? You know about this concept of centuries-old Serbian homes.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know you don't like history but people in Bosnia are really hung up on history. I have to tell you very briefly, talking about Srebrenica. It was named Srebrenica after silver mines, silver being "srebro," and the first money minted by the Serbian king Milutin was made in Srebrenica, and the Dubrovnik merchants traded precisely with those coins minted at Srebrenica. I don't know what Krstic meant but what I'm talking about was in the 13th century. And all the way until the Ottoman invasion into the Balkans, Bosnia was Christian, and this sign drawn here, you characterised it earlier as a Serbian nationalistic sign. Now, on the coat of arms of Serbia from 1835, there is a two-headed eagle taken over from the times of the division of the Roman empire into the western and the eastern, and this is a symbol from ancient Serbian history. And even in communist times, this symbol with the four Ss and the cross existed. What Krstic wanted to show, I really don't know. I know that Srebrenica and Zepa are in Republika Srpska in Bosnia and Herzegovina and Muslims still live there today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I've heard the version that everyone in Bosnia is Serbian and that the Muslims are Serbian, they were just cowards that were taken over by Islam and that is what this reference has to do with. Am I wrong?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's partly true, I mean there is some truth in that. It was the period of Islamisation, forcible conversion of Christians to Islam. I said that one brother in a family converted to Islam; another brother remained a Christian. All the way until the 1963 Constitution, the Muslims declared themselves as Serbs or Croats of Muslim faith. It was only after the '74 constitution that they started declaring themselves in censuses as of Muslim ethnicity, and today they call themselves Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you in your report talked about expelling the enemy from centuries-old Serbian homes. In the context where your superior orders said to force the Muslim local population to leave, what did you mean when you said "expel the enemy from their homes," the Serbian homes?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the person who wrote that report on my behalf, I don't know what they meant. Did the moral guidance organ tell him to write that or did he write it on his own initiative? I don't know. But he is responsible to me for what he wrote and I am responsible to others. If I had written that report myself, I certainly wouldn't have written that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You're not suggesting that General Gvero, Colonel Saravic and Nenad Simic came down to your brigade and in some kind of conspiracy sent out of this kind of message without the commander having any responsibility for it, are you? Sounds familiar to me.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said that. I said the moral guidance organ is responsible to me as well as all the other assistants and I am responsible to my superiors for both what I do myself and for what they do. So I'm not trying to insinuate that somebody else is responsible. I am responsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's look at 65 ter 4236. March 2nd, 1993, another of your reports to the corps. Number one says: "In the course of the night and the morning, the enemy did not display fiercer activities apart from occasional breach of silence at some parts of the front-line. At around 8.30 hours, columns of civilians and soldiers with pack animals were noticed from Udrc and Rasevo towards Konjevic Polje. The columns were hit with every available means." So this column of civilians and soldiers and pack animals, when you say "every available means," you must mean artillery.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Already in the end of February, and early in March and throughout -- sorry, early in February and almost all the way through March, a large number of armed people dressed as civilians were trying to break through towards Tuzla and there was no great difference by that time between those in civilian clothes and those in uniform. That column was observable from a great distance, over 2 kilometres because there was a canyon in between of the Drinjaca River so the battalion in Drinjaca could see them. They had infantry weapons and they had mortars of 60- and 82-millimetres. Whether they fired mortars at them or not, I don't know, but a mixed column of this composition, under the regulations and the international humanitarian law, I repeat, is a legitimate military target.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, if they were soldiers dressed as civilians, you're right. But this doesn't say that. This says "civilians and soldiers." You want to just edit it to throw in civilians -- soldiers dressed as civilians?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That also is a possibility, able-bodied men. If the man next to one of them is killed, he will take his rifle and continue fighting. We can look up international humanitarian law and see what military target is defined as and we'll see all of what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: One more document. 65 ter 4258, March 2nd, 1993. So it's the same day. This is the -- you can keep that one if it may be helpful, General. This is the Drina Corps report to the Main Staff. We see in the B/C/S page 1 and English page 1, basically the repetition of what you had reported. "At about 8.30 hours in the zone of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade, a column of soldiers and pack animals was seen moving from Mount Urdc and Rasevo village in the direction of Konjevic Polje village. Fire was opened on the column." There's been an editing job by the corps, hasn't there?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what we read here. But at that time when people went with pack animals, they went to fetch equipment and weapons from Kalesija and another place and brought them to Cerska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think we better stop there, General, and -- it's time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to make a comment, I waited until the end of the day to make this comment from the questions that have been put to the witness by the Prosecution, showing him documents and asking questions as to whether civilians were fired upon. What is missing in all of these questions, Mr. President, is that is the Prosecution saying that these documents are evidence of crimes and does he have any evidence that these were criminal actions; and if he doesn't have any such evidence or if he has such evidence, they should be shown to the witness so at least the witness can say. But right now, he's simply making suggestions of crimes without putting any evidence whatsoever to the witness, and it's wholly inappropriate, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll deal with this tomorrow if you wish to respond, Mr. McCloskey. We stand adjourned until tomorrow, 9.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 26th day of February, 2009, at 9.00 a.m. 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.46 p.m.,
